content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with the planners and presenters of this report, have disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. However, there are two exceptions: Barbara Body, who is employed by LabCorp and serves on the Advisory Board of Becton Dickinson, Roche Diagnostic Systems, and Roche Molecular Systems, and Nancy Strockbine, who has conducted research with Inverness Medical Innovations. The presentations will not include any discussion of the unlabeled use of a product or investigational use of a product. Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infections are a significant public health concern in the United States, causing approximately 100,000 illnesses, 3,000 hospitalizations, and 90 deaths annually, based on the most recent estimates from 1999. The majority of reported STEC infections in the U.S. are caused by E. coli O157:H7, with an estimated 73,000 cases occurring each year. Non-O157 STEC bacteria are also important causes of diarrheal illness, with at least 150 serotypes associated with outbreaks and sporadic cases. In the U.S., six non-O157 serogroups (O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, and O145) account for most reported non-O157 STEC infections. The toxins produced by STEC are named for their structural and functional similarity to Shiga toxins produced by Shigella dysenteriae type 1. Shiga toxin 1 (Stx1) is neutralized by antibodies against Shiga toxin, whereas Shiga toxin 2 (Stx2) is not neutralized by these antibodies but is neutralized by homologous antibodies. STEC are also referred to as verocytotoxigenic E. coli (VTEC), and those causing human illness are often called enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC). In this report, all E. coli that produce Shiga toxin are referred to as STEC. STEC serotypes are named based on their somatic (O) and flagellar (H) antigens. For simplicity, all STEC with the O antigen 157 are referred to as O157 STEC, regardless of whether the H7 antigen has been identified or Shiga toxin production has been confirmed. STEC with other O antigens are referred to as non-O157 STEC or by their specific O antigen. STEC infections typically cause acute diarrhea, which is often bloody. Approximately 8% of individuals diagnosed with O157 STEC infection develop hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a life-threatening condition characterized by thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and renal failure. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a syndrome with similar signs and symptoms to HUS, is typically diagnosed in adults. When TTP follows a diarrheal illness, it is usually caused by infection with O157 STEC or another STEC. In this report, TTP diagnosed after a diarrheal illness is referred to as HUS, regardless of the patient’s age. The progression of illness to HUS depends on the virulence of the infecting strain and host factors. While most cases of diarrhea-associated HUS are linked to O157 STEC, certain non-O157 STEC strains can also lead to HUS. Non-O157 STEC strains that produce only Stx2 are more frequently associated with HUS than strains that produce only Stx1 or both Stx1 and Stx2. STEC infections and HUS can occur in individuals of all ages, but the incidence of STEC infection is highest in children under 5 years old, as is the risk for HUS. Although STEC infections are more common during the summer months, they can occur year-round. Both O157 STEC and O111 STEC have a low infectious dose (<100 organisms). Prompt and accurate diagnosis of STEC infection is critical because early treatment with parenteral volume expansion may reduce renal damage and improve patient outcomes. Additionally, antibiotic therapy in patients with STEC infections may be associated with more severe disease, making prompt diagnosis essential to ensure appropriate treatment. Rapid laboratory identification of STEC strains is also crucial for implementing control measures, responding effectively to outbreaks, detecting new and emerging serotypes, and monitoring disease epidemiology trends. Most O157 STEC isolates can be readily identified in the laboratory when grown on sorbitol-containing selective media because O157 STEC cannot ferment sorbitol within 24 hours. However, many clinical laboratories do not routinely culture stool specimens for O157 STEC. Furthermore, selective and differential media are not available for culturing non-O157 STEC, and even fewer laboratories culture stool specimens for these bacteria. The increased use of enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect Shiga toxin or the genes encoding the toxins (stx1 and stx2) has facilitated the diagnosis of both O157 and non-O157 STEC infections. Simultaneous stool culture for O157 STEC and EIA testing for Shiga toxin is more effective for identifying STEC infections than using either technique alone. Because virtually all O157 STEC have the genes for Stx2 (stx2) and intimin (eae), which are associated with severe disease, detection of O157 STEC should prompt immediate steps such as parenteral volume expansion to reduce the risk of renal damage in the patient and prevent the spread of infection to others. Guidelines for clinical and laboratory identification of STEC infections have been previously published. This report provides the first comprehensive and detailed recommendations for the isolation and identification of STEC by clinical laboratories. These recommendations are intended primarily for clinical laboratories but also serve as an important reference for healthcare providers, public health laboratories, public health authorities, and patients and their advocates. Stool specimens from patients with acute onset of community-acquired diarrhea and from patients with possible HUS should be tested for STEC. Testing should not be limited to specific patient groups (e.g., children) or specific times of the year (e.g., summer months).
